notes: In r11, http2-goaway-last-stream-retry replaces http2-tcp-loss-stream-blocking to avoid mirroring r12's stream-independence fact. In r12, qpack-blocked-field-section replaces qpack-cross-stream-ordering to avoid testing stream independence again.

cards.statement: An origin server should keep several Set-Cookie fields separate in an HTTP response.
cards.explanation: Combining Set-Cookie fields with commas can change their meaning because cookie syntax already uses commas.

cards.statement: A user agent separates cookie name-value pairs with semicolons in the Cookie request field.
cards.explanation: The Cookie field separates successive cookie pairs with a semicolon and a space.

cards.statement: A user agent includes a cookie's Path attribute alongside its value in the Cookie request field.
cards.explanation: The Cookie request field omits the attributes supplied with Set-Cookie. The server does not receive the cookie's Path attribute in that field.
cards.misconception: Cookie requests return stored cookie attributes alongside their values.

cards.statement: A user agent replaces a stored cookie after accepting another with the same name, domain and path.
cards.explanation: The name, domain and path identify the stored cookie. An accepted cookie with the same combination takes its place.

cards.statement: A user agent gives a cookie subdomain scope by default when the server omits Domain.
cards.explanation: Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie. Its host must exactly match the request host for the cookie to be selected.
cards.misconception: Omitting Domain extends a cookie's host scope to subdomains.

source.title: RFC 6265, Sections 5.3 and 5.4: Storage and Sending

cards.statement: A user agent may accept `Domain=example.com` on a cookie set by `shop.example.com`.
cards.explanation: The host shop.example.com domain-matches example.com. A server can therefore set a cookie with that parent domain.

cards.statement: A user agent defaults a cookie's Path to `/guide/page.html` for a request to `/guide/page.html`.
cards.explanation: For /guide/page.html, RFC 6265's default-path algorithm yields /guide by removing the final slash and the portion after it.
cards.misconception: A cookie's default path includes the request path's final file component.

cards.statement: A server deletes a stored cookie by setting its value to an empty string.
cards.explanation: An empty cookie value can remain stored. To request deletion, the server sends a matching cookie with an expiry in the past.
cards.misconception: An empty cookie value acts as a deletion instruction.

cards.statement: A user agent may evict a stored cookie before its specified expiry time because of memory pressure.
cards.explanation: Expiry sets a maximum lifetime, not guaranteed retention. A user agent may remove cookies earlier because of resource limits or user preferences.

cards.statement: RFC 6265 uses the setting server's port as a matching condition when a user agent selects outgoing cookies.
cards.explanation: Cookies are shared across ports on a host. Cookie scope does not include the port on which the server set the cookie.
cards.misconception: Cookie delivery matches the port that originally set the cookie.

cards.statement: A cookie-enabled user agent processes Set-Cookie fields in HTTP error responses.
cards.explanation: An HTTP error status does not itself suppress Set-Cookie processing. Cookie-enabled user agents process these fields subject to cookie acceptance policies.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser lets scripts read Set-Cookie through response.headers on a same-origin response.
cards.explanation: The Fetch Standard filters Set-Cookie from response headers exposed to scripts, including on same-origin responses.
cards.misconception: Scripts can read a same-origin network response's Set-Cookie field through fetch().

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may use just the path and query as the target of a GET sent to a forward proxy.
cards.explanation: For a GET sent to a forward proxy, HTTP/1.1 requires an absolute-form target, including the URI's scheme and authority.
cards.misconception: A forward-proxy request uses the same path-only target as a direct origin request.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server answers a request that omits Host with 400 Bad Request.
cards.explanation: RFC 9112 requires 400 Bad Request when an HTTP/1.1 request omits Host, even if the target URI appears elsewhere.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient treats a connection as persistent by default.
cards.explanation: The HTTP/1.1 persistence default lets later requests reuse the connection after the current response.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.0 client requests persistence by sending a Keep-Alive field alone.
cards.explanation: HTTP/1.0 persistence is negotiated with the keep-alive option in Connection. A Keep-Alive field alone does not request it.
cards.misconception: The Keep-Alive field itself activates persistence in HTTP/1.0.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient can detect the end of chunked content while keeping the connection open.
cards.explanation: Chunked framing signals message completion independently of a closed connection, so a recipient can retain the connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may delimit its request content by closing the connection.
cards.explanation: HTTP/1.1 request content needs explicit framing by length or transfer coding; connection closure does not delimit it.
cards.misconception: Connection closure serves as a valid framing delimiter for HTTP/1.1 request content.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient uses Content-Length ahead of Transfer-Encoding when both fields occur.
cards.explanation: Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length. RFC 9112 says a message carrying both fields ought to be handled as an error.
cards.misconception: Content-Length takes priority over Transfer-Encoding when both occur.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server may answer a chunked request with 411 when it requires Content-Length.
cards.explanation: A server may reject request content that lacks Content-Length with 411, including content framed with chunked transfer coding.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server returns pipelined responses in the order their processing finishes.
cards.explanation: A server sends responses to pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests in request order, even if it processes safe requests in parallel.
cards.misconception: Pipelined HTTP/1.1 responses can be returned in completion order.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 proxy removes fields named by Connection before forwarding an HTTP message.
cards.explanation: A forwarding proxy removes fields nominated by Connection because those fields apply to the incoming connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server names the selected protocol in Upgrade when it sends 101 Switching Protocols.
cards.explanation: A 101 response must include Upgrade to identify the protocol selected for the existing connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may use Upgrade to move the conversation from TCP to UDP.
cards.explanation: Upgrade changes the protocol running over the existing connection. It does not replace the connection's transport protocol.
cards.misconception: Upgrade replaces the underlying transport along with the application protocol.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a client can interleave several request streams over a single TCP connection.
cards.explanation: Separate HTTP exchanges use separate streams whose frames share one connection, allowing requests to overlap.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, an endpoint may charge a HEADERS frame against its advertised stream flow-control window.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 flow control governs DATA frames. HEADERS frames do not consume the advertised flow-control window.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 flow control applies to header transmission as well as content transmission.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a recipient treats an uppercase letter in a field name as making the message malformed.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 senders lowercase field names, and recipients treat an uppercase field name as a malformed message.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a sender places pseudo-header fields after the regular fields in a header section.
cards.explanation: A sender puts pseudo-header fields before regular fields. A pseudo-header appearing after a regular field makes the message malformed.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 pseudo-header fields follow ordinary fields.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a server conveys a response's numeric status code in the `:status` pseudo-header field.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 defines :status for response control data. A response needs this field, including an interim response.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 proxy can send `Connection: close` to end persistence after its response.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 prohibits the Connection field. An HTTP/2 message containing it is malformed.
cards.misconception: HTTP/1.1's Connection field remains usable for HTTP/2 connection management.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a client must make an included Host identify the same authority as `:authority`.
cards.explanation: A client must not send Host identifying a different authority from :authority. Their values are normalized for comparison.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 server treats a POST whose content-length differs from its DATA content size as malformed.
cards.explanation: For a message carrying content, content-length has to match the total content conveyed in DATA frames.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 client selects `h2` through the Upgrade field when establishing an HTTPS connection.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 over TLS selects h2 through the TLS ALPN extension during connection establishment.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 over HTTPS uses HTTP Upgrade for protocol selection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 client may reuse an HTTPS connection across origins when the server has authority for both.
cards.explanation: Connection reuse across HTTPS origins depends on server authority, including a certificate valid for the new origin's host.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 proxy chosen by the client may generate 421 for an origin it lacks authority to serve.
cards.explanation: A proxy must not generate 421. An origin server or its gateway uses 421 to reject a target URI outside its authority or connection context.
cards.misconception: A proxy can generate 421 to reject a request for an origin it cannot authoritatively serve.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 client reads GOAWAY's last-stream ID as proof that the server completed that request.
cards.explanation: The last-stream ID marks the highest stream the sender might have processed. It does not confirm that the corresponding request completed.
cards.misconception: GOAWAY's last-stream ID identifies the last completed request.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client carries QUIC traffic over TCP when it connects to an origin server.
cards.explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. Its reliable transport comes from QUIC rather than a TCP connection.
cards.misconception: HTTP/3 keeps TCP as the transport beneath QUIC.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client uses QUIC's integrated TLS 1.3 handshake to establish its connection.
cards.explanation: QUIC incorporates TLS 1.3 into connection establishment, combining cryptographic and transport negotiation.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 receiver can make progress on another stream while packet loss blocks one request stream.
cards.explanation: QUIC supplies reliability per stream, so loss affecting one stream does not impose a connection-wide delivery stall.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client may wait for QPACK table updates before decoding a response's headers.
cards.explanation: A field section can remain blocked while the decoder waits for referenced dynamic-table entries to arrive on the QPACK encoder stream.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client may directly access an `http` URI's authoritative server over QUIC.
cards.explanation: HTTP/3 cannot directly access an http URI's authoritative server. Such access needs another mechanism to identify an authoritative HTTP/3 service.
cards.misconception: HTTP/3 can use the usual http URI authority directly over QUIC.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client can use connection IDs to retain its QUIC connection when its network address changes.
cards.explanation: Connection IDs let QUIC associate packets with an existing connection despite changes to the client's address or network path.

cards.statement: A server may answer an early-data request with 425 when processing it risks replay.
cards.explanation: A 425 Too Early response signals that the server declines the risk of processing a request that might be replayed.

source.title: RFC 8470, Section 5.2: The 425 (Too Early) Status Code

cards.statement: A user agent groups `http://example.com:443` and `https://example.com:443` into the same origin.
cards.explanation: The http and https schemes identify distinct origins with separate namespaces, even when the host names match.
cards.misconception: Matching host names make http and https URLs part of one origin.

cards.statement: A client using Alt-Svc treats the alternative service's host as the resource's new origin.
cards.explanation: Alt-Svc changes the connection route while the URI's original scheme, host and port continue to identify the resource's origin.
cards.misconception: Using an alternative service changes the origin that identifies the resource.

cards.statement: A client can authenticate an Alt-Svc endpoint on another host using a certificate valid for that host alone.
cards.explanation: An Alt-Svc alternative must prove authority for the origin's host. A certificate covering just its different network host is insufficient.
cards.misconception: An alternative service's certificate needs to cover its own host rather than the origin's host.

cards.statement: A client treats an Alt-Svc advertisement as fresh for 24 hours by default from message generation.
cards.explanation: Alt-Svc advertisements have a 24-hour freshness lifetime unless the ma parameter supplies a different lifetime.

source.title: RFC 7838, Section 3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

cards.statement: A client treats `persist=1` as extending an Alt-Svc entry beyond its advertised freshness lifetime.
cards.explanation: The persist=1 parameter signals usefulness across network changes. It does not extend the entry's freshness lifetime.
cards.misconception: The persist parameter keeps an Alt-Svc entry usable after its freshness expires.

source.title: RFC 7838, Section 3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values
